screens.title: Inheritance: Building Hierarchies
screens.narratorSegment: Welcome. In this lesson we explore inheritance in C++, the mechanism that lets a new class build on an existing one and express an "is-a" relationship. You'll learn why inheritance reduces duplicated code, how the three access forms — public, protected and private — change what a derived class can use and expose, and the guaranteed order in which constructors and destructors run. We'll see concrete examples such as an Animal and Dog pair and a library example with Book and Magazine, so you can connect the concept to code you will write. You'll also meet common pitfalls: forgetting to call the correct base constructor, assuming private members are visible to children, and overusing deep hierarchies when composition fits better. By the end of the chapter you'll be able to design a simple hierarchy, implement constructors that forward initialization to base classes, and reason about member access and cleanup order. As you progress, think about whether a relationship is truly "is-a" or instead "has-a"; that question often prevents brittle designs. Ready to explore access rules, constructor order, and a hands-on shape exercise? Let's dive into inheritance and see how small, clear hierarchies make code easier to reuse and maintain.

Second, you'll learn to tell public, protected and private inheritance apart and predict how each one changes member accessibility from within derived classes and from outside code. Third, you'll describe and trace the order constructors and destructors run in an inheritance chain so you can reason about initialization and cleanup correctly. screens.title: What is Inheritance?
screens.narratorSegment: Inheritance in C++ is a language mechanism that lets you create a new class based on an existing one so the new class reuses fields and methods rather than redefining them. The central idea is the "is-a" relationship: a derived class is a specialized form of its base. For example, a Dog is an Animal; we give Animal common members like a name and basic behaviors such as eat and sleep, and Dog adds breed and bark. This avoids copying shared code across types and keeps behaviour centralized. A common misconception is treating inheritance as a general reuse tool for any shared code; instead, check whether a true specialization exists. If classes share behavior but do not represent a subtype relationship, composition is often a clearer choice. Practically, you declare inheritance in C++ using a colon and an access specifier followed by the base class name. When you read code, use three quick checks: does the derived type make sense as a subtype conceptually, does it need to expose the base interface, and are base members appropriate for reuse or meant to be independent? Example: Book as a base for Magazine fits because both can be borrowed and have titles; Magazine then adds issueNumber. Takeaway: use inheritance to model true specializations, centralize shared code, and keep hierarchies shallow for maintainability.

keyIdea.text: Inheritance models specialization (is-a) and centralizes shared members so derived types extend base behavior rather than duplicate it.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › What is Inheritance?
Definition

Inheritance and the "is-a" idea

Inheritance lets a derived class reuse attributes and methods from a base class and add specialized behavior.

Concrete example
Animal defines name, eat(), sleep(); Dog inherits these, adds breed and bark(). This reduces duplicate code across animal types.
Common misconception
Inheritance is not a general reuse tool. Ask whether a true subtype relationship exists; if not, prefer composition.
Why it matters
Correctly used inheritance centralizes shared behavior, simplifies maintenance, and clarifies intent in your class designs.
Analogy & Visual
Book → Magazine

Book has title, author, ISBN, borrow() and returnBook(). Magazine can inherit those and add issueNumber and publicationDate, removing duplication.

Quick checks
  • Is the relationship truly a specialization?
  • Will derived objects need the base interface publicly?
  • Can initialization be forwarded correctly?
Key Takeaway
Use inheritance to model clear subtype relationships, centralize shared behavior, and avoid deep hierarchies that complicate maintenance.

screens.title: Public, Protected, Private Inheritance
screens.narratorSegment: C++ offers three inheritance access specifiers — public, protected and private — and each one alters how base class members are seen in derived classes and by external code. Public inheritance preserves the original interface: base public members remain public in the derived class, and protected remain protected; private members are never directly visible to children. This models the classic "is-a" relationship, where users of the derived type can still use the base's public A P I. Protected inheritance converts both public and protected base members into protected members of the derived class; they are accessible inside the derived class and its descendants but hidden from outside users. Private inheritance transforms base public and protected members into private members of the derived class, hiding the base interface from outside code and making the base serve purely as an implementation detail that the derived class can use internally. A typical misconception is thinking private inheritance creates a has-a relationship automatically; while private inheritance hides the base interface, composition where an object contains a base instance is often clearer to express true ownership or contained relationships. Use public inheritance when the derived type should be usable anywhere the base is used, protected when you need to expose behavior to further descendants only, and private when you explicitly want to hide the base interface but reuse its implementation.

keyIdea.title: Access rules
keyIdea.text: Public preserves base interface, protected hides it from outside but exposes to descendants, private hides the base interface from outsiders entirely.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Access Specifiers

Public vs Protected vs Private

Each specifier changes what derived classes and outside code can access. Below are side-by-side cards showing impacts and a small example.

Public Inheritance
Base public → derived public. Base protected → derived protected. Derived objects expose base interface. Use for true "is-a".
Protected Inheritance
Base public and protected become protected in derived. Accessible to further derived classes but not to external code.
Private Inheritance
Base public and protected become private in derived. External code cannot use the base interface through derived objects.
Concrete code snippet
class Dog : public Animal {
public:
    // inherits public and protected members as same access
};

class Special : private Animal {
    // Animal's public members become private here
};
Example Card
Why it matters

Choose public when derived objects should be used as base objects. Use private only when you want to reuse implementation but hide the base interface from users of the derived class.

Key Takeaway

Access specifiers control visibility of inherited members; pick the one that matches intended external exposure and extension needs.

screens.title: Animal and Dog — Constructor Example
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the Animal and Dog example to see constructor and destructor ordering as well as how a derived constructor forwards initialization to the base. In the example, Animal defines a constructor that accepts a name and prints when it's called. Dog inherits publicly from Animal and in Dog's constructor initializer list it calls the Animal constructor with the name, then initializes its own breed field. When you construct a Dog object, the runtime first calls Animal's constructor so the base portion of the object is properly initialized. After that returns, the Dog constructor runs to finish derived-specific setup. On destruction this order reverses: Dog's destructor is invoked first, then Animal's destructor runs to clean up base resources. A common mistake is omitting the call to the base constructor when the base has only parameterized constructors; this causes a compilation error because the compiler cannot call a missing default constructor. The concrete example shows printed output that reveals the order: you will see the Animal constructor message, then Dog constructor, and when the object goes out of scope you will see Dog destructor followed by Animal destructor. Practice tracing these messages while writing constructors to validate initialization behavior.

keyIdea.title: Constructor order
keyIdea.text: Base constructors run before derived constructors; destructors run in reverse order to ensure safe initialization and cleanup.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Constructor Order
Code Example
#include <iostream>
#include <string>

class Animal {
public:
    std::string name;
    Animal(const std::string& n) : name(n) {
        std::cout << "Animal constructor called for " << name << std::endl;
    }
    ~Animal() { std::cout << "Animal destructor called for " << name << std::endl; }
};

class Dog : public Animal {
public:
    std::string breed;
    Dog(const std::string& n, const std::string& b) : Animal(n), breed(b) {
        std::cout << "Dog constructor called for " << name << " (" << breed << ")" << std::endl;
    }
    ~Dog() { std::cout << "Dog destructor called for " << name << std::endl; }
};

int main() {
    Dog myDog("Buddy", "Golden Retriever");
    return 0;
}
Explanation & Trace
  • When myDog is created, Animal constructor runs first to initialize base fields.
  • Dog constructor runs next to initialize breed and derived behavior.
  • When myDog goes out of scope, Dog destructor runs first, then Animal destructor.
Key Takeaway

Always ensure base initialization is performed, especially when base constructors require arguments. Trace printed messages to confirm the order.

screens.title: Calling Base Constructors: Initializer Lists
screens.narratorSegment: When a base class requires parameters in its constructor, derived classes must explicitly call that constructor in their initializer lists. If you do not, the compiler attempts to call a non-existent default constructor and you will get a compilation error. For example, in the Dog constructor we call the Animal constructor with the name parameter before initializing breed. The syntax places the base call immediately after the derived constructor signature and a colon, then lists initializers separated by commas. This pattern guarantees the base subobject is initialized with the intended values before derived initialization begins. In practical terms, always inspect the base class constructors when deriving; if the base only has parameterized constructors, plan to forward the required parameters from the derived constructor. A common misconception is that assignment inside the derived constructor body will initialize base members; it will not. The base must be initialized in the initializer list. This matter becomes more important as hierarchies add fields that require immediate initialization, such as references, const members, or resources. Takeaway: use initializer lists to forward values and avoid missing-constructor errors.

keyIdea.title: Initializer list
keyIdea.text: Use the derived constructor initializer list to call base constructors and initialize base subobjects with required parameters.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Initializer Lists
Pattern
Dog(const std::string& n, const std::string& b) : Animal(n), breed(b) {
    // derived construction
}
Initializer lists ensure the base Animal is constructed with n before Dog initializes breed. Using assignment inside the body cannot substitute for this sequence.
Example & Pitfall

If Animal only has a parameterized constructor and you omit calling it, the code will not compile. Always inspect base constructors and forward parameters accordingly.

Common mistake

Forgetting to call the base constructor causes a missing default constructor error at compile time when no no-arg base constructor exists.

screens.title: Private Inheritance vs Composition
screens.narratorSegment: Private inheritance makes the base class's public and protected members private in the derived class, effectively hiding the base interface from users of the derived type. This can be useful when you want to reuse implementation but do not want to promise the base's interface to outside code. However, a frequent design suggestion is to prefer composition over private inheritance when the relationship is actually "has-a" or when you want clearer ownership semantics. Composition explicitly shows containment and avoids surprising access changes, while private inheritance can obscure intent because it still models an inheritance relationship at the language level. A misconception is assuming private inheritance is equivalent to composition; it is not identical. Use private inheritance when you need to reuse protected members or override protected behavior, but choose composition when you simply want to include and delegate to another object. The practical rule: if the derived object should not be used as the base type by external code, and you only need internal reuse, either private inheritance or composition can work—evaluate which one better communicates intent and supports maintainability.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Private Inheritance vs Composition

Private inheritance

Hides the base interface; derived class can use base implementation internally but external users cannot use the base API through the derived object.

When to consider
When reuse is needed without exposing the base's operations to callers, or when you want to override protected behavior used internally.
Why prefer composition often
Composition communicates ownership clearly and avoids surprises caused by inherited members changing access levels.

Composition example

Instead of inheriting Engine privately, a Car can contain an Engine member. This makes the relationship explicit and easier to reason about.

Key Takeaway

Use private inheritance sparingly. Prefer composition when the relation is ownership or containment for clearer, more maintainable designs.

screens.title: Shape Hierarchy: Circle and Rectangle
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on activity asks you to implement a Shape base class with a protected color and two derived shapes: Circle and Rectangle. Shape has a constructor that initializes color and a displayColor method. Circle must inherit publicly from Shape, keep radius private, and call the Shape constructor from its initializer list. Its calculateArea method returns pi times radius squared. Rectangle is similar: it stores width and height and returns width times height for area. A typical student flow is: first implement Shape's constructor and displayColor, then create Circle's constructor using the initializer list to call Shape with the color parameter before initializing radius, and finally implement calculateArea. A common misconception is trying to set the base's protected member by assignment in the body rather than forwarding via the initializer list when required. After implementing both derived classes, create objects in main, call displayColor and calculateArea on each, and verify outputs. This exercise reinforces constructor forwarding, protected visibility for shared state, and correct area calculations for each shape. Carrying out the activity confirms you can both design and implement small hierarchies safely.

keyIdea.title: Activity focus
keyIdea.text: Implement Shape with protected color, then Circle and Rectangle that forward color via initializer lists and provide area computations.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Shape Hierarchy
Starter & Solution
Below is a completed implementation matching the activity steps: Shape with protected color; Circle and Rectangle call the base constructor and implement calculateArea.
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <cmath> // For M_PI

class Shape {
protected:
    std::string color;
public:
    Shape(const std::string& c) : color(c) {
        std::cout << "Shape constructor called for color: " << color << std::endl;
    }
    void displayColor() const {
        std::cout << "This shape is " << color << "." << std::endl;
    }
    ~Shape() {
        std::cout << "Shape destructor called for color: " << color << std::endl;
    }
};

class Circle : public Shape {
private:
    double radius;
public:
    Circle(const std::string& c, double r) : Shape(c), radius(r) {
        std::cout << "Circle constructor called for a " << color << " circle." << std::endl;
    }
    double calculateArea() const { return M_PI * radius * radius; }
    ~Circle() { std::cout << "Circle destructor called for a " << color << " circle." << std::endl; }
};

class Rectangle : public Shape {
private:
    double width;
    double height;
public:
    Rectangle(const std::string& c, double w, double h) : Shape(c), width(w), height(h) {
        std::cout << "Rectangle constructor called for a " << color << " rectangle." << std::endl;
    }
    double calculateArea() const { return width * height; }
    ~Rectangle() { std::cout << "Rectangle destructor called for a " << color << " rectangle." << std::endl; }
};

int main() {
    Circle myCircle("Red", 5.0);
    Rectangle myRectangle("Blue", 4.0, 6.0);
    myCircle.displayColor();
    std::cout << "Circle area: " << myCircle.calculateArea() << std::endl;
    myRectangle.displayColor();
    std::cout << "Rectangle area: " << myRectangle.calculateArea() << std::endl;
    return 0;
}
Explanation
  • Shape's constructor sets the protected color and prints a message to confirm initialization.
  • Circle and Rectangle call Shape(c) in their initializer lists so color is set before derived setup.
  • calculateArea implements formulas from the activity: pi·r² for Circle and width·height for Rectangle.
Key Takeaway

Follow the activity steps to practice initializer lists and protected members; run the main to observe constructor and destructor ordering.

screens.title: Designing a Clear Class Hierarchy
screens.narratorSegment: Designing a hierarchy starts with a simple sequence of decisions and checks. Step one: ask whether the relationship is truly an "is-a" semantic. If a Car is a Vehicle, inheritance fits; if a Car has an Engine, prefer composition. Step two: decide which members belong in the base class so common attributes and behaviors are centralized. screens.title: Pitfalls and Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: As you work with inheritance, several practical pitfalls appear repeatedly. One is forgetting to explicitly call a base constructor that requires parameters. If the base has no default constructor and you omit the call in the derived initializer list, the code will not compile. Another is attempting to directly access private base members from a derived class — private means private to that class only; use protected if you want child classes to read or modify a member while keeping it inaccessible to external code. Overusing deep inheritance hierarchies is another danger: long chains make reasoning about where behavior lives and where state is initialized more difficult. Prefer composition when the relationship is ownership or containment. Finally, if you plan to delete derived objects through base pointers later, remember the base should have a virtual destructor — that point is noted here and will be covered in the polymorphism chapter. Best practices: keep hierarchies shallow, initialize bases intentionally via initializer lists, use protected sparingly for targeted extension, and favor composition when subtype semantics do not truly hold. Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Pitfalls & Best Practices
Common Pitfalls
  • Omitting a base constructor call when the base has no default constructor — causes compile-time errors.
  • Trying to access private base members from derived classes — private is not inherited.
  • Deep inheritance chains that make code brittle and hard to maintain.
  • Not preparing for polymorphic deletion by declaring a virtual destructor in base classes when needed.
Best Practices
  1. Keep hierarchies shallow and focused on specialization.
  2. Use protected for members that should be inherited but not public.
  3. Prefer composition when an object owns another rather than modeling a subtype.
  4. Always forward required base parameters via initializer lists.
Key Takeaway

Check constructors and access levels early. Design choices now prevent many maintenance headaches later.

screens.title: Assessing Constructor/Destructor Order and Access
screens.narratorSegment: Let's analyze two short assessment items to practice tracing constructor and destructor order and reasoning about access. First, consider a Base and Derived where Derived inherits publicly. When Derived is instantiated, the Base constructor runs first, then Derived's constructor. At program exit or when the object goes out of scope, destructors run in reverse: Derived destructor first, then Base destructor. The printed output therefore shows Base Constructor, Derived Constructor, Derived Destructor, Base Destructor. Second, consider a Vehicle base class with a private engineType and a protected maxSpeed, and a Car derived publicly. Derived classes cannot access private members of their base, but they can access protected members. So Car can access maxSpeed but not engineType directly. A common error is to assume private members are visible to children; that is not the case. Use protected if you want derived types to use base state but keep it hidden from external code. These two analyses reinforce constructor lifecycle and member visibility rules you will use frequently when reading or writing class hierarchies. fullNarratorScript:
Welcome. In this lesson we explore inheritance in C++, the mechanism that lets a new class build on an existing one and express an "is-a" relationship. You'll learn why inheritance reduces duplicated code, how the three access forms — public, protected and private — change what a derived class can use and expose, and the guaranteed order in which constructors and destructors run. We'll see concrete examples such as an Animal and Dog pair and a library example with Book and Magazine, so you can connect the concept to code you will write. You'll also meet common pitfalls: forgetting to call the correct base constructor, assuming private members are visible to children, and overusing deep hierarchies when composition fits better. By the end of the chapter you'll be able to design a simple hierarchy, implement constructors that forward initialization to base classes, and reason about member access and cleanup order. As you progress, think about whether a relationship is truly "is-a" or instead "has-a"; that question often prevents brittle designs. Ready to explore access rules, constructor order, and a hands-on shape exercise? Let's dive into inheritance and see how small, clear hierarchies make code easier to reuse and maintain.

In the next screens we set clear goals to make your work with inheritance practical. First, you'll be able to explain inheritance and the "is-a" idea so you can decide when to reuse code versus when to compose behavior. Second, you'll learn to tell public, protected and private inheritance apart and predict how each one changes member accessibility from within derived classes and from outside code. Third, you'll describe and trace the order constructors and destructors run in an inheritance chain so you can reason about initialization and cleanup correctly. Fourth, you'll implement basic hierarchies in C++, writing base and derived classes with correct constructor forwarding. Each objective is paired with a short why-it-matters statement and a simple visual hint to help you remember. These competencies together let you create clear, maintainable hierarchies and avoid errors like assuming private members are available to child classes. Keep these objectives in mind as we work through examples and hands-on code; they will guide the code you write and the tests you run.

These additional objectives prepare you to write robust hierarchies and avoid common mistakes. First, you will identify pitfalls such as attempting to access private base members from a derived class, or forgetting to call a base constructor that requires parameters. Second, you'll implement the provided Shape activity: a Shape base class with a protected color, and Circle and Rectangle derived classes that call the base constructor and supply area methods. Third, you'll recognize when inheritance hides a base interface via private inheritance, and how that differs from composition which we will study later. Fourth, you'll be alert to an important practical note: if you intend to use polymorphism, a virtual destructor in the base class is necessary; this chapter flags that point and directs you to the next chapter for full coverage. Each objective pairs a practical example with a short mnemonic so you can quickly test your understanding while coding and reading error messages.

Inheritance in C++ is a language mechanism that lets you create a new class based on an existing one so the new class reuses fields and methods rather than redefining them. The central idea is the "is-a" relationship: a derived class is a specialized form of its base. For example, a Dog is an Animal; we give Animal common members like a name and basic behaviors such as eat and sleep, and Dog adds breed and bark. This avoids copying shared code across types and keeps behaviour centralized. A common misconception is treating inheritance as a general reuse tool for any shared code; instead, check whether a true specialization exists. If classes share behavior but do not represent a subtype relationship, composition is often a clearer choice. Practically, you declare inheritance in C++ using a colon and an access specifier followed by the base class name. When you read code, use three quick checks: does the derived type make sense as a subtype conceptually, does it need to expose the base interface, and are base members appropriate for reuse or meant to be independent? Example: Book as a base for Magazine fits because both can be borrowed and have titles; Magazine then adds issueNumber. Takeaway: use inheritance to model true specializations, centralize shared code, and keep hierarchies shallow for maintainability.

C++ offers three inheritance access specifiers — public, protected and private — and each one alters how base class members are seen in derived classes and by external code. Public inheritance preserves the original interface: base public members remain public in the derived class, and protected remain protected; private members are never directly visible to children. This models the classic "is-a" relationship, where users of the derived type can still use the base's public A P I. Protected inheritance converts both public and protected base members into protected members of the derived class; they are accessible inside the derived class and its descendants but hidden from outside users. Private inheritance transforms base public and protected members into private members of the derived class, hiding the base interface from outside code and making the base serve purely as an implementation detail that the derived class can use internally. A typical misconception is thinking private inheritance creates a has-a relationship automatically; while private inheritance hides the base interface, composition where an object contains a base instance is often clearer to express true ownership or contained relationships. Use public inheritance when the derived type should be usable anywhere the base is used, protected when you need to expose behavior to further descendants only, and private when you explicitly want to hide the base interface but reuse its implementation.

Let's walk through the Animal and Dog example to see constructor and destructor ordering as well as how a derived constructor forwards initialization to the base. In the example, Animal defines a constructor that accepts a name and prints when it's called. Dog inherits publicly from Animal and in Dog's constructor initializer list it calls the Animal constructor with the name, then initializes its own breed field. When you construct a Dog object, the runtime first calls Animal's constructor so the base portion of the object is properly initialized. After that returns, the Dog constructor runs to finish derived-specific setup. On destruction this order reverses: Dog's destructor is invoked first, then Animal's destructor runs to clean up base resources. A common mistake is omitting the call to the base constructor when the base has only parameterized constructors; this causes a compilation error because the compiler cannot call a missing default constructor. The concrete example shows printed output that reveals the order: you will see the Animal constructor message, then Dog constructor, and when the object goes out of scope you will see Dog destructor followed by Animal destructor. Practice tracing these messages while writing constructors to validate initialization behavior.

When a base class requires parameters in its constructor, derived classes must explicitly call that constructor in their initializer lists. If you do not, the compiler attempts to call a non-existent default constructor and you will get a compilation error. For example, in the Dog constructor we call the Animal constructor with the name parameter before initializing breed. The syntax places the base call immediately after the derived constructor signature and a colon, then lists initializers separated by commas. This pattern guarantees the base subobject is initialized with the intended values before derived initialization begins. In practical terms, always inspect the base class constructors when deriving; if the base only has parameterized constructors, plan to forward the required parameters from the derived constructor. A common misconception is that assignment inside the derived constructor body will initialize base members; it will not. The base must be initialized in the initializer list. This matter becomes more important as hierarchies add fields that require immediate initialization, such as references, const members, or resources. Takeaway: use initializer lists to forward values and avoid missing-constructor errors.

Private inheritance makes the base class's public and protected members private in the derived class, effectively hiding the base interface from users of the derived type. This can be useful when you want to reuse implementation but do not want to promise the base's interface to outside code. However, a frequent design suggestion is to prefer composition over private inheritance when the relationship is actually "has-a" or when you want clearer ownership semantics. Composition explicitly shows containment and avoids surprising access changes, while private inheritance can obscure intent because it still models an inheritance relationship at the language level. A misconception is assuming private inheritance is equivalent to composition; it is not identical. Use private inheritance when you need to reuse protected members or override protected behavior, but choose composition when you simply want to include and delegate to another object. The practical rule: if the derived object should not be used as the base type by external code, and you only need internal reuse, either private inheritance or composition can work—evaluate which one better communicates intent and supports maintainability.

This hands-on activity asks you to implement a Shape base class with a protected color and two derived shapes: Circle and Rectangle. Shape has a constructor that initializes color and a displayColor method. Circle must inherit publicly from Shape, keep radius private, and call the Shape constructor from its initializer list. Its calculateArea method returns pi times radius squared. Rectangle is similar: it stores width and height and returns width times height for area. A typical student flow is: first implement Shape's constructor and displayColor, then create Circle's constructor using the initializer list to call Shape with the color parameter before initializing radius, and finally implement calculateArea. A common misconception is trying to set the base's protected member by assignment in the body rather than forwarding via the initializer list when required. After implementing both derived classes, create objects in main, call displayColor and calculateArea on each, and verify outputs. This exercise reinforces constructor forwarding, protected visibility for shared state, and correct area calculations for each shape. Carrying out the activity confirms you can both design and implement small hierarchies safely.

Review the essential ideas: inheritance models an "is-a" relationship and centralizes shared behavior so derived classes can extend base functionality. Public inheritance preserves the base interface, protected inheritance converts base public and protected to protected in the derived class, and private inheritance converts them to private, hiding the base interface from external users. Constructors run from base to derived and destructors run from derived to base; use initializer lists to forward required base parameters and avoid compilation errors. Watch for common pitfalls: attempting to access private base members, forgetting to call a parameterized base constructor, and overusing deep hierarchies when composition would be clearer. Before you finish, remember three compact ideas. First, inheritance models specialization: a derived type should conceptually be a base type. Second, access specifiers govern visibility: public preserves the interface, protected offers descendant-only access, and private hides the base interface from users. Third, always plan initialization: forward required base parameters using initializer lists and expect destructors to run in reverse order.
